translations.text: After Saul died, David came back from slaughtering the Amalekites, and he stayed in Ziklag for only two days.
On the third day a man came from Saul's army. His tunic was torn and he had poured earth on his head. When he came before David, he fell to the ground and bowed down to him.
David said to him, "Where have you come from?" He said, "From the people of Israel. I escaped from the slaughter."
David said to him, "What happened? Tell me!" He told him, "The people fled from the battle. Many of the people fell, and Saul and his sons were killed."
David answered and said to the man, "Come forward and tell me how you know that Saul and his son Jonathan are dead."

The man told him: "A large troop attacked Saul's troop, and they cut each other down on Mount Gilboa. They set upon [?] Saul, and I saw that he was leaning on his spear. When the commanders and the charioteers were turned away [?] from him,
Saul looked back at me and called me, and I said, "Here I am!"
He said to me, "Who are you?" I told him, "I am an Amalekite!"
He said to me, "Come, kill me, for a dreadful darkness has covered my eyes, and my soul still moves in my body!"
So I killed him, because I knew he could not survive. After he fell, I took the diadem from his head and the bracelet from his arm, and I have brought them to my lord."
When David heard this, he took hold of his collar and tore his clothes, and so did every man who was with him.
They wept and mourned, and they fasted until evening for Saul, for his son Jonathan, for the people of Judah, and for the house of Israel, because they had fallen by the edge of the sword.
David said to the man who had told him these things, "Where are you from?" He answered, "I am the son of an Amalekite man, a foreigner who came to live here."
David said to him, "How were you not afraid to raise your hand and kill the Lord's anointed?"
David called one of the men and said to him, "Go, strike him down!" He went at once, struck him, and killed him.
David said to him, "Your blood be on your own head, because your own mouth testified against you when you said, 'I killed the Lord's anointed!'"
David mourned and sang a lament over Saul and his son Jonathan.
He ordered that it be taught to the sons of Israel and of Judah. It was written in the holy books, and he said:
"Know this truly, Israel, about your people who fell wounded: how the mighty fell wounded in battle!

Do not tell it in Gath, and do not tell it in the streets of Ashkelon, so that the daughters of the foreigners do not hear it and rejoice and celebrate, and the daughters of the uncircumcised do not shout for joy!

You mountains of Gilboa! May no morning dew fall on you, and may no gentle rain come down on you from the clouds. You mountains, mountains of death, because on you the shields of the mighty fell. Saul's shield was not anointed with oil.
It was anointed with the blood of warriors and the fat of brave men instead. Jonathan's arrows did not turn back in vain, and Saul's sword did not return empty to its sheath!"
Saul and Jonathan, beloved and beautiful, who were not divided from one another in their life, were not divided in death either: higher than eagles and braver than lions.
You daughters of Israel! Weep for Saul, who adorned you with purple clothing and with ornaments of gold to adorn you.
How the mighty have fallen in battle by wounds! Jonathan, you were wounded unto death, to my grief [?]!
I grieve, I grieve for you, Jonathan, my brother, to look upon that beauty of yours, for you were beloved to me, you who were greater and better to me than the love of the beauty of women!
How the mighty have fallen in battle, and how suddenly that desirable vessel has perished!

After this David inquired of the Lord and said, "Is it permitted for me to go up to one of the cities of Judea?" The Lord said to him, "Go up." And David said, "Where shall I go?" The Lord said to him, "To Hebron."
So David went up to Hebron, and his two wives with him: Ahinoam the Israelite, and Abigail, the wife of Nabal, of Carmel.
And the men who were with him went, each with his household, and settled in Hebron.
And the men of Judah came and gathered to him, and there they anointed David king over Judah. And they told David, saying, "The men of Jabesh-gilead came and took away Saul and buried him."

And David sent messengers to the leaders of Jabesh-gilead and said to them, "Blessed are you by the Lord, for you have done a good deed: you remembered the love of Saul, your lord, and showed kindness to him and buried him.
May the Lord show mercy and truth to you! And I too will do good to you, because you have fulfilled the word that was spoken.
And now let your hands be strong, and be sons of valor, for although Saul your lord has died, now, behold, the house of Judah has anointed me king over them."
And Abner the son of Ner, the commander of Saul's army, took Mephibosheth, the son of Saul, and brought him across into the camp.
And he made him king over Gilead, over Jezreel, over Israel, over Ephraim, over Manasseh, and over all Israel.
Mephibosheth, the son of Saul, was forty years old when he became king over Israel, and he reigned over them for two years. But those who were of the house of Judah followed David.
And the number of the days of David, as long as he reigned in Hebron, was seven years and six months.
And Abner the son of Ner went out, and the servants of Mephibosheth, the son of Saul, with him, from the camp of the hill.

And Joab the son of Zeruiah went out from Hebron, and the servants of David with him, and they met one another at the pools of the Gibeonites, and they sat down, these on one side and those on the other.
Abner began to speak to Joab and said to him, "Let the young men arise and sport with one another among us, before us!" And Joab said, "Let them arise."
And they arose and came forward by number: twelve of the sons of Benjamin, the servants of Mephibosheth, the son of Saul, and twelve of the servants of David.

And they fought one against another as equals: with his left hand each seized the other's hair, and with his right hand thrust his sword into his opponent's side, and at once struck him down. And that place was named "Portion of the Ardabags [?]", which is in Gibeon.
And the battle grew fierce that day, and Abner was defeated and fled before the servants of David.
And the three sons of Zeruiah were there: Joab and Abishai and Asahel. And Asahel was swift of foot, like a gazelle of the field.
Abner fled from Asahel, and Asahel pursued him and did not let him turn aside to the right or to the left.
Abner looked back at Asahel and said to him: "Are you Asahel?" And he said to him: "I am. Look, I am overtaking you!"
Abner answered: "Turn away from me, to the right or to the left, and kill one of these servants, whichever you want, and take his spoils!" But Asahel would not agree to turn away from him.
And Abner said to him a second time: "Stand away from me, or I may kill you. Then how could I look your brother Joab in the face?"

But Asahel did not stand back. So Abner turned on him and struck him in the belly with a spear, and it came out through his back, and he died. And when the pursuers came up and saw Asahel dead, they stopped there and pursued no further.
Then Joab and Abishai pursued Abner until sunset. When the sun had gone down and it grew dark, they came to the foot of Ammah.
And the sons of Benjamin gathered together and formed a large band and went up onto a great hill.

And from that hill Abner called out to Joab and said: "Must that sword of yours be let loose without restraint? Or do you not know that at the end of this business it brings bitterness? How long will you refuse to turn your people back from slaughtering their brothers?"
Joab answered: "As the Lord lives, if you had not spoken that word, you would have seen the hand of all my people, each one against his brother."
Joab ordered the trumpet to be blown, and all the people halted and pursued Israel no further, and fought no more.
And Abner and his people went westward all that night and came to the bank of the Jordan. They crossed over and spread out along the whole riverbank until they reached the camp of the Midianites.
And Joab turned back and gathered all David's people and inspected them, and nineteen men were found to have been killed, Asahel among them.
And David's servants had killed three hundred and sixty men of the sons of Benjamin, from Abner's people.
And they took Asahel and buried him in his father's tomb at Bethlehem. And Joab and the people who were with him set out and travelled all night, and dawn broke on them at Hebron.

And the struggle of war between the house of Saul and the house of David grew fierce. And the house of David grew greater and stronger as time went on, while the house of Saul dwindled and grew weaker.
And six sons were born to David in Hebron. His firstborn was Amnon, by Ahinoam the Israelite.
And his second was Daluia, by Abigail of Carmel; the third was Absalom, the son of Maacah, the daughter of Talmai, king of Geshur.
And the fourth was Adonijah, the son of Haggith; and the fifth was Shephatiah, by Abital;
and the sixth was Ithream, by Eglah, David's wife. These were born to David in Hebron.
And the struggle of the war grew stronger between the house of Saul and the house of David, and Abner was master and ruler over the house of Saul.
Saul had taken a concubine, and her name was Rizpah, daughter of Siba. Mephibosheth, the son of Saul, began to speak to Abner and said to him: "Why did you take my father's concubine?"

Abner was very angry with Mephibosheth because of this word, and he said to him: "Am I some dog? [?] I did all this of my own accord. I showed kindness to the house of your father, to his brothers and to his kindred, and I did not turn away and go over to the house of David. And now you have risen up to take vengeance on me for the sake of one woman's [?].
May the Lord do this to me and add more to it, if I do not do for David as the Lord swore to him!
For today the Lord has taken the kingdom from the house of Saul and has set up the throne of David over Israel and over the house of Judah, from Dan to Beersheba."
And Mephibosheth was afraid because of this word, and because of that fear he could not answer Abner a single word.
And Abner sent messengers to David at Hebron and said to him: "Make a covenant with me, and I will give you my hand, and I will turn all Israel over to you to serve you."

And David said: "Yes, it is good; I will do so. I will make a covenant with him and confirm it with him. But I tell you one thing: you shall not see my face again unless you bring with you Michal, the daughter of Saul, when you come to meet me."
And David sent messengers to Mephibosheth, the son of Saul, and said: "Give me my wife Michal, whom I won with the hundred of the uncircumcised Philistines."
And Mephibosheth sent and took her from her husband Paltiah, the son of Selmia.

Her husband followed his wife, weeping, and went with her as far as Barakid. Then Abner said to him: "How long will you keep following? Turn back and go!" And at once he turned back at the word of Abner.
And Abner spoke to the elders of Israel and said: "Yesterday and the day before you were seeking David, and you wanted him as king over you.

Now fulfil your wish, and come and present yourselves before him, for the Lord himself spoke about David and said: 'By the hand of David my servant I will save my people Israel from the hands of the Philistines and from the hands of their enemies!'"
Abner said this to all the sons of Benjamin. And Abner came to David at Hebron to tell him everything that seemed good in the eyes of Israel and in the eyes of the sons of Benjamin.
And Abner came to David at Hebron to tell him, and with him only twenty men, and David made a great feast for Abner and for the men who had come with him.

Abner answered and said to David: "Let me go, and I will go and gather all Israel to my lord, and I will lay down my covenant with you, and you will reign over all whom your soul desires!" And David dismissed Abner, and he went away in peace.

And at that very moment David's servants and Joab came, and they arrived from the camp with a great deal of plunder that they had with them. And Abner was not with David at Hebron, for David had dismissed him and sent him away in peace.
And when Joab and all the people who were with him heard, they told Joab: "Abner son of Ner came to David, and he let him go and sent him away in peace."
And at once Joab went in to the king and said to him: "What is this thing you have done? Abner son of Ner came to you, and you released him, and he went away in peace?
Do you not know the wickedness of Abner son of Ner? He came to you to deceive you, to observe your going out and your coming in, and to find out what you are doing."
And Joab went out from David and sent messengers after Abner, and they brought him back from the well of Sirah; and David did not know.

And Abner returned to Hebron, and Joab came to meet him and drew him aside [?] toward the gates, and spoke with him deceitfully, and stabbed him in his side, and at once killed him. And Abner died in return for the blood of his brother Asahel.
After this, when David heard, he said: "I and this kingdom of mine are innocent before the Lord of that blood for ever and ever.

But the blood of Abner son of Ner be upon the head of Joab and upon all his father's house. And may the house of Joab never be without one who has a discharge [?], and a leper, and a beggar for bread, and one who dies by the sword and by famine."
And Abishai and Joab had always been watching for a chance to kill Abner in return for the blood of Asahel their brother, who was killed in the battle at Gibeon.

And David said to Joab and to all the people who were with him: "Put your hands to your collars and tear them, take off your ornaments, put on sackcloth, and mourn for Abner." And King David himself walked in front of Abner's bier.
And they buried him in Hebron. And King David lifted up his voice over Abner's tomb and made all the people weep.
He cried aloud and lamented, saying: "Abner died the way Nabal died.
His hands were not bound, nor were his feet put in fetters; but like Nabal he fell before the children of lawlessness."

And all the people gathered to comfort David and to press him to eat bread while it was still day. David swore an oath and said: "May God do so and so to me, for until the sun goes down I will not taste bread or any other food."
When all the people heard this, everything that David did before all the people pleased them.
And on that day they understood that the death of Abner son of Ner had not been by the king's command.
The king spoke to the people and said: "Do you not know that a great prince has died today in Israel?

Or do you not know today that a kinsman and friend and great ruler has fallen? But these men, the sons of Zeruiah, are harder of heart in cruelty than I am. May the Lord repay those who do evil for their wickedness."
When Mephibosheth son of Saul heard that Abner had died in Hebron, the sinews of his hands went slack, and all the people of Israel were alarmed.
And at once two men, captains of the troops of Mephibosheth son of Saul: Baanah and Rechab, the sons of Rimmon the Beerothite, of the sons of Benjamin.
For the Beerothites had fled [?] to Gittaim and have lived there to this day.

And Jonathan, the son of Saul, had one surviving son, who was lame in his feet. He was five years old, because at the time when the [?] (news) of Saul and of Jonathan his son came from Jerusalem, his nurse picked him up and ran off with him. And as she fled in haste, she fell on the child's feet and lamed him. His name was Mephibaal.
And the sons of Rimmon the Beerothite, Rechab and his brother Baanah, came and went to the house of Mephibosheth. He was sleeping in his own bedchamber during the heat of the day, right at midday.
His doorkeeper, who guarded the doors, had also grown drowsy and was sleeping at the door. And Rechab and Baanah, the two brothers, went in secretly.
While Mephibosheth was sleeping in his bedchamber, they struck him and killed him on the spot. They cut off his head and carried it off along the western road all night long.

And they brought the head of Mephibosheth to David at Hebron and said to the king: "Here is the head of Mephibosheth, the son of Saul, your enemy, who sought to take your life. The Lord has given the lord our king vengeance on his enemies: on Saul, his enemy, and on all his family."
David answered Rechab and his brother Baanah, the sons of Rimmon, and said to them: "As my Lord lives, who has delivered my soul from all distress!

There was the man who told me about the death of Saul and Jonathan. He thought he was bringing me some kind of good news, and they seized him right there in Ziklag and killed him. Who knows, perhaps I ought to have given him some reward for his news.
So now too, these wicked men went and killed a righteous man in his own bedchamber. In the same way I will seek vengeance for his blood at their hands, and I will wipe them off the earth!"

And David gave orders to his servants, and they killed them immediately. They cut off their hands and feet and hung them up at the tower in Hebron. And they took the head of Mephibosheth and buried it in the tomb of Abner in Hebron.
And all the tribes of Israel came and gathered to David at Hebron and said to him: "We are bone of your bones and flesh of your flesh.
For before this, in times past, while King Saul was still alive, it was you who were the leader and commander of Israel. For the Lord said to you: 'You shall shepherd my people Israel!'"
And all the elders came and gathered to David at Hebron, and King David made a covenant with them at Hebron before the Lord. And they anointed David king over all Israel.
For David was thirty years old when they anointed him king, and he reigned for forty years.
For he reigned over Judah at Hebron for seven years and six months, and over Israel he reigned for thirty-two years, and six months over all Israel and Judah.

And King David and all his men went with him to Jerusalem, to the Jebusite who lived in all that land. And David was told that the Jebusites were saying: "David shall not come in here, for the blind and the lame have risen up to attack him." They were also saying: "Do not let David come down here!"
And he captured the stronghold of Zion and said: "This is the city of David!"

And on that day David gave a command, saying: "Everyone who strikes down the Jebusites, let him raise the sword against the blind and the lame, and let him destroy those who hated David's soul." This is why it has become a saying: "The blind and the lame shall not enter the house of the Lord!"
And David settled in the stronghold, and it was called the City of David. He built the city around the hill, and his own house was built inside it.
And David kept advancing and growing greater, and the Lord Almighty was with him.
And Hiram, king of Tyre, sent messengers to him, and sent him fir and pine timber. He also sent him carpenters and stonemasons, and they built a house there for David.
And David understood that the Lord had made his kingship over Israel prosper and had set it on a straight course, and he knew that the Lord had raised his kingdom high over all the people of Israel.
And after he came from Hebron, David took more wives and concubines in Jerusalem, and more sons and daughters were born to David in Jerusalem.
And these are the names of his children who were born to him, thirteen children: Shammua, Iesseban [?], Nathan, Solomon,
Ibhar, Elishua, Elphadat [?], Nogah,
Nepheg, Minat [?], Samis [?], Beeliada, Eliphelet.

And the Philistines heard that David had been anointed king over Israel. So the Philistines rose up and came out to look for David. When David heard that the Philistines were looking for him, he went out and came down toward the stronghold.
And the Philistines came and spread out across the Valley of the Titans.
David asked the Lord, saying: "Should I go up against the Philistines? Will you give them into my hands?" And the Lord said to David: "Go up, for I will surely give them into your hands."

And David went and attacked them at the Slope of Slaughter and destroyed them. And David said: "The Lord has destroyed my enemies the Philistines before me, as many waters split and break through." This is why that place was called the Slope of Slaughter.
And as they fled, the Philistines left their idols behind. David's people picked them up, and David said: "Burn them with fire right there on the spot."
Then the Philistines came out once more, as a large gathered force, into the valley of the Plain of the Titans.
And David asked the Lord, and the Lord said to him: "Do not go out against them directly. Instead, circle around and hide close to them in the Valley of Mourning.

And when you hear the sound of movement in the place of mourning, only then rush out against them into the fight, for then the Lord will go out ahead of you to strike down the Philistines in the battle."
And David did exactly as the Lord had commanded him, and he struck down the Philistines from Gibeon all the way to Gezer.
And David held an assembly of the people. He gathered all the chosen men of the house of Israel, about seventy thousand men.

And David set out, and all the people with him, along with the wealthy men and the leaders of the house of Judah, to go up onto the hill and bring from there the ark of the covenant. The name of the Lord of hosts was called upon this ark, and the cherubim had come down and stood on it.
And they set the ark of the covenant on a new cart and carried it away from the house of Abinadab, which was on the hill.
Uzzah and his brothers, the sons of Abinadab, were bringing the cart with the ark of God. Uzzah and his brothers walked around the ark, in front of it and behind it, and alongside the ark of God.
David and all the people of Israel were making music before the ark of the covenant with pipes, harps, drums, [?] and cymbals, and with the many different songs of the singers.
They came as far as the threshing floor of Ornan the Jebusite. At that moment Uzzah put out his hand to the ark of the covenant of God to steady it, because the oxen had jolted it.

The Lord grew angry with Uzzah and struck him down on the spot for his irreverent boldness. He died there beside the ark of the Lord, before the Lord, because he had dared to stretch out his hand freely to the ark of the covenant of God.
David was grieved at the striking-down that had fallen on Uzzah, and that place was given the name "The Striking-Down of Uzzah" to this day.
David was afraid of the Lord that day and said: "How can I take this ark of the covenant of the Lord God into my house?"
The ark of God arrived, but David did not want to bring the ark of the covenant of the Lord to his own place. Instead, David turned it aside to the house of Abinadab the Gittite.
The Lord blessed the house of Abinadab and everything that belonged to him because of the ark of God.

They told David: "God has blessed the house of Abinadab and everything that belongs to him because of the ark of God." David spoke up and said: "I will go and bring the blessing of the Lord into my house." David went and brought the ark of the covenant of the Lord up from the house of Obed-edom (Abedad) to the city of David.
With him, among those carrying the ark of the Lord, were seven companies of singers, along with sacrifices of bullocks and lambs.
David danced before the ark [?] among the pipers and drummers, before the Lord, dressed in purple garments.
David himself and all Israel were bringing the ark of the Lord to the city of David.
Michal, Saul's daughter, was looking out through the window. When she saw King David singing, rejoicing and dancing to the sound of the pipe before the ark of the Lord, she despised him in her heart.
They brought in the ark of the Lord and set it in the place that David had set up for it, and David offered a peace offering before the Lord.
When David had finished offering the offerings, the peace sacrifices, he blessed the people before the Lord Almighty.

He divided portions among all the people and handed them out equally to all Israel, from Dan to Beersheba, to each one, men and women alike: one loaf of bread, one portion of meat and one [?] from the pan. Then all the people went home, each to his own house.

David returned home to bless his household. Michal, Saul's daughter, came out to meet David. She greeted him and said: "How elegant and glorious you were today, when you went about uncovered in front of your servants and maidservants! You were as uncovered today as someone who strips himself bare in his dancing."

David answered Michal and said to her: "I was rejoicing and dancing before my Lord. As the Lord my God lives, who chose me over your father and over all his house and established me as ruler over all this people of his, Israel, I will rejoice and make merry and dance before the Lord, and I will strip myself before the Lord in joy more and more.
"And now I have appeared contemptible in your eyes and in the eyes of your maidservants, in whose presence you said to me: 'How glorious you appeared!'"
And Michal, the daughter of Saul, had no child until the day of her death.
And it happened, when David had settled in his own house and the Lord had given him rest from all his enemies around him,
that the king answered the prophet Nathan and said to him: "Look, I live in houses of cedar, but the ark of the Lord stands inside the tent of the Lord."
The prophet Nathan answered the king and said to him: "Wherever God has given you success, do everything that is in your heart, for the Lord your God is with you."
And on that day the command of the Lord came to the prophet Nathan, and he said:
"Go and tell my servant David, 'Here is what the Lord says: You shall not build me a house for me to dwell in.'

"For I have not dwelt anywhere in dwellings from the day and the time when I brought the children of Israel out of the land of the Egyptians until this time. Instead I went with them in their camps, in a tent,

"in every place where I went with the children of Israel. And did I ever say a word to anyone from any of the tribes of the children of Israel whom I commanded to shepherd my people Israel, saying: 'Why have you not built me a house of cedar wood, hewn with four walls and joined with planks?'
"And now say this to my servant David: 'Here is what the Lord Almighty says: I took you from the sheepfold, from the flocks of sheep, and made you leader of my people Israel.'

"And I was with you on all the ways that you went, and I destroyed your enemies before your face, and I gave you a great name, like the names of the great ones who were before you on the face of the earth.

"And I will give a place to my people Israel. I will plant them, establish them, and settle them in their own place, and they will no longer be anxious. And the son of lawlessness will no longer afflict them again as he did before,
"from the time when I appointed judges over my people Israel. And now I will give you rest from all your enemies, and the Lord will make known to you how the building of his temple is to be.

"And it will happen, when your days are completed and you are gathered to your fathers, that I will raise up one of your offspring, who will come from your own body, and I will prepare for him the establishment of his kingdom.
"He will build a temple for my name, and I will set up his throne for ages without end.

"And I will be a father to him, and he will be a son to me. And if his lawlessness appears before me, I will punish him with the rod of men, and I will discipline him with the merciful correction of the sons of men."
But I will not take my mercy away from him, as I did with those whom I removed from before my face.
And I will establish his kingdom and his way forever before me, and his throne shall be set up before me forever.
And Nathan spoke to David according to all these words and according to all this vision.
And King David went in and sat before the Lord and said: "Who am I, O my Lord, or what is my name, that you have loved me so much?

For this is worthless and nothing before you, O Lord, my Lord! And you have spoken so far into the future about the house of your servant, and this is the law of your servant toward you, O Lord, my Lord!
And what more can David add to say before you? And now you know, O Lord, your servant and your people!
And now, by your own heart, you have done all this greatness, to make your servant understand your riches, O Lord, my Lord!
For there is no one like you, and there is no God at all besides you, according to all that we have heard with our ears.

Or who is like your people Israel, whom you led on the earth, O God, to gain them as a people for yourself? And you magnified your name with great majesty when you brought out your people, whom you delivered from the land of the Egyptians: the people and the inheritance.
You prepared for yourself your people Israel as a people forever, and you, Lord, became their God!
And now, O Lord my God, let the word that you spoke about your servant be confirmed forever and ever, and do as you have spoken.
And now let your name be exalted forever and ever, O Lord Almighty, God of Israel, and let the house of David your servant be exalted before you!

For you, O Lord Almighty, God of Israel, opened the ear of your servant and said: 'I will build you up!' Therefore your servant has found boldness from God to pray this request to you. And I have prayed before you;
and now, O Lord my God, you are God, and your words shall stand in truth, as you have spoken these good things about your servant.
And now begin, and bless the house of your servant, so that it may remain forever before you; for you, Lord, have spoken, and with your blessing let the house of your servant be blessed forever."
And after all this, David struck down the Philistines and subdued them, and David took the land that had been set apart out of the hands of the Philistines.

And David struck down Moab and measured out their land with a measuring line, for he made them lie down on the ground. Two portions were cut down for death, and he took the third portion alive. And the rest of Moab became servants of David and brought him tribute.

Then David struck down Hadadezer the son of Rehob, the king of Zobah, for he had gathered an army and was coming to lay his hands on the bank of the river Euphrates. David struck him down and slaughtered him.

And he took from him as captives a thousand chariots, seven thousand horsemen, and twenty thousand light-armed shield-bearers. And he disabled all the chariots, but he picked out a hundred gold-plated chariots and kept them for royal service.
At that time the Syrian came to support Hadadezer, king of Zobah. Then David slew twenty-two thousand fighting men of the Syrian.

David set up garrisons in place after place in the lands toward Syria and toward Damascus. He made the land of the Syrians his servants, and they always brought him gifts and tribute. The Lord helped David in all his ways, wherever he went.

David took the golden quivers that Hadadezer, king of Zobah, had worn, and all the spoil: the gilded chain mail and the golden spear. He carried it all to Jerusalem. This was what Shishak, king of the Egyptians, took away at the time he captured Jerusalem, in the days of Rehoboam, son of Solomon.

From Matebak and from the other chosen cities of Hadadezer, King David brought away a great quantity of bronze. From it King Solomon made the bronze temple, the bronze pillars, the brass basins and all the tin [?] of its vessels.
Eliab, king of the Hamathites, heard that David had slain and destroyed all the forces of Hadadezer.

He sent Iedura, his son, from Hamath to King David to ask after his peace, because he had destroyed all the forces of Hadadezer, and to bless him, for Hadadezer had always been at war with him. So Iedura, son of Eliab king of the Hamathites, came to David with a great gift of gold and silver and many vessels of bronze.
King David received it and dedicated it to the Lord, together with the gold and silver and all the vessels he had taken from the cities that he had taken by great force:
from the Edomites and the Moabites, from the sons of Ammon, from the foreigners and from the people of the Amalekites, and from the spoil of Hadadezer, king of Zobah.
David made a name for himself in all the land. Then, after his return, he slew the Idumeans, and at Engemelek eighty thousand fighting men.

He made the lands pay tribute. David built fortresses in the land of the Idumeans, summoned [?] workers and set up monuments, and the inhabitants of Idumea became David's servants. The Lord helped David in all his ways, wherever he went.
David reigned over all Israel, and David did justice and judgment for all his people.
Joab, son of Zeruiah, was commander over all the people of Israel, and Jehoshaphat, son of Ahilud, was the recorder of the chronicles.
Zadok, son of Ahitub, and Abimelech, son of Abiathar, were his priests, and Seraiah was chief of the scribes.
Benaiah, son of Jehoiada, was counsellor, and Ophilti and Okereti, sons of David, were his court overseers.
Then David began to speak and said: "Is anyone left of the house of Saul, so that I may show him kindness for the sake of Jonathan, my beloved?"

One man was left of the house of Saul, and his name was Ziba. They summoned him before David. The king began to speak to him and said: "Are you the servant Ziba?" He answered and said: "I am, your servant!"

The king said to him: "Is there anyone still left of the house of Saul, an heir of his house, so that I may show kindness to him?" Ziba answered the king and said: "There is a son of Jonathan who is lame in his feet."
David said: "Where is he?" Ziba said: "In the house of Machir son of Ammiel, in Lo-debar."
King David sent and brought him from the house of Machir son of Ammiel, from Lo-debar.
They brought Mephibosheth, the son of Jonathan son of King Saul. He fell on his face and bowed down to him. Mephibosheth said to him: "Here I am, your servant!"

David said to him: "Do not be afraid, for I will surely show you kindness for the sake of your father Jonathan. I will give you all the estate of Saul, your grandfather, and you will always eat bread at my table."
He bowed down to him and said: "What am I, your servant, that you have looked on me, a dead dog such as I am?"
King David summoned Ziba, Saul's servant, and said to him: "All that was Saul's property and all the plunder I have given to your master's son."

"You, with your sons and your servants, shall work the land for him, and gather the produce for your master, and look after the stores [?], so that they may eat. And Mephibosheth, your master's son, shall always eat bread at my table." Ziba had fifteen sons and twenty servants.
Ziba answered the king and said: "Whatever my lord commands his servant, I will do." And Mephibosheth always ate at the king's table like one of his own children.
Mephibosheth had a young son named Mica. And all the household and estate of Ziba's house served Mephibosheth.
Mephibosheth lived in Jerusalem, because he had received the king's command that he should always be given his bread. He himself was lame in both feet.
After this, the king of the Ammonites died, and his son Hanun became king in his father's place.

David spoke and said: "I will show kindness to Hanun son of Nahash, as his father did to me." So David sent his servants to comfort him about his father. David's servants went and arrived in the land of the Ammonites.

The princes of the Ammonites answered Hanun, their lord, and said to him: "David has not sent these comforters out of any respect, to honor your father. No, he has sent them as spies of the ways in and out of this city of yours, so that they may search out what is inside and outside it. That is why these servants of David have come to you."
When Hanun heard this, he seized David's servants and ordered that half of their hair and beards be shaved off. He cut off the skirts of their tunics and sent them away.

When David heard about these men, he sent men to meet them. They saw that the men had been greatly disgraced, and he said: "Stay there in Jericho until your hair and beards have grown back, and only then come."

When the Ammonites saw that David's servants had been insulted and put to shame, the Ammonites sent and hired the Syrian people of Beth-rehob and the Syrians of Zobah, twenty thousand foot soldiers [?], the king of Maacah with a thousand men, and Ish-tob with two thousand men.
And when King David heard this, he sent Joab, his commander-in-chief, and all his army with him.

And the sons of Ammon came out, made ready, and drew up in battle order before the gates of their city. The Syrians, Beth-rehob, Zestob [?] (probably Ish-tob) and Maacah drew up separately in the open field.

When Joab saw that they were drawn up and ready against his battle line, both in front of it and behind it, he picked out all the young fighting men of the sons of Israel, and came and drew them up facing the Syrians.
And he gave all the rest of the army to Abishai, his brother, who brought them and drew them up facing the sons of Ammon.
And Joab said to Abishai, his brother: "If the Syrian grows too strong and overpowers me, you come to my aid. If the sons of Ammon overpower you, then I will come to help you!"
"Be brave, be strong! Let us fight this army that has come against us, for the sake of the cities of our God, and may the Lord God do what is good for us in his sight!"
When Joab had said these words, he gathered all the army together into one body. With great force in the fight he attacked the Syrians, and at once he put them to flight and drove them into the city.

When the sons of Ammon saw that the Syrians had been put to flight, they too fled from Abishai and went into the city. When Joab saw that he had driven them in flight into the city, he turned back and went to Jerusalem.
When the sons of Ammon saw that the Syrians had fled before the sons of Israel, they gathered together.

And Hadadezer sent word and called out the Syrians who were beyond the river at Kalmas [?] (perhaps Chalamak). And the Khuzhiks [?], Elam and Suba [?] came, with Shobach (Sabeth) and Hadadezer's commanders leading them.
When David learned of this, he ordered all the army of the sons of Israel to gather. They crossed the river Jordan and came to Lalam (Helam). The Syrians drew up facing David and fought against him.

And the Syrians fled before Israel. David killed seven hundred of the Syrian horsemen, who were spa-razeni [?] (possibly armoured cavalry), and forty thousand mkwirtskhli [?] shield-bearing foot soldiers. And they killed their commander Shobach (Sabeth).

When all the kings who had come to help Hadadezer saw that he had been defeated by the sons of Israel, they made a covenant, bowed their necks, and submitted as servants to the sons of Israel. And the Syrians were afraid and no longer came to help the sons of Ammon.

And in the following year, at the time when kings go out to war, David sent Joab and all the army of Israel. They destroyed all the sons of Ammon, then surrounded and besieged the city of Rabbah. And David stayed in Jerusalem.

One day David had gone out in the evening. David came out from his resting place and walked about on the roof of the royal palace. From the roof he saw a woman bathing in her garden, and the woman was very beautiful.
And David sent someone to find out about the woman. Her name was Bathsheba. She was the daughter of Eliah (Eliam) and the wife of Uriah the Hittite.
And David sent messengers and brought that woman, and he went in to her and lay with her. She had only just washed herself from her uncleanness. And she went to her own house,
having conceived by him. And she sent to David and said: "Know that I have conceived by you!"
At that time David sent to Joab and said to him: "Send me Uriah the Hittite at once!" And Joab sent him at once.
And Uriah came to David. David began to question Uriah and said: "Is Joab well?" And he said: "Well!" Then he spoke again and said: "Are the people well?" And he said: "They are well!"
And David said to Uriah: "Come now [?], go to your house, wash your feet and rest!" And Uriah went out from the king's presence and came to the king's servants,
and he slept among them at the gates of the king's palace, with the servants of his lord. And he did not go to his own house.
And they told King David: "Uriah did not go to his house." David said to Uriah: "Have you not come from a journey? Why did you not go into your house?"

Uriah answered David and said: "If the ark of the covenant of the Lord and all the people of Israel and of Judah are living outside in tents, and my lord Joab and all his people are out in the field, how could I go into my house to eat and drink with my wife? I swear by your sun and by the love of your own life that I will not do this thing!"
And David said to Uriah: "Stay here today, and tomorrow I will send you off." And Uriah stayed in Jerusalem that day. And on the next day

David called him and fed him at his table. He ate and drank before the king, made merry and got drunk. And when evening came, he went out and lay down with the servants of the gates, with the servants of his lord.
And the next day, as soon as it was dawn, David wrote a letter and sent it to Joab by the hand of Uriah.
And in the letter he wrote thus: "Set Uriah toward the heaviest fighting, and do not you go forward with him. Leave him, so that they kill him."
And when Joab was besieging that city, he set him at a place where the fighting was fiercest, where the city's valiant fighters were.
And the strong men of that city sallied out and fought against Joab. And many of his people fell in that clash, at the word of David, and they also killed Uriah the Hittite.
And Joab sent messengers to David.
And he commanded the man thus: "When you give your report to the king, begin your account with the severity of the battle.
And if he becomes angry over the slaughter of the people and says to you: 'Why did you go near the wall? Did you not know that disorderly slaughter comes down on the people from above?

Who killed Abimelech son of Jerubbaal? Did not one woman throw down a piece of a millstone, strike him and kill him at Thebez?' And when he says this, answer him: 'The battle grew heavy against us, and a troop sallied out of the city, and we turned in flight, and then we drove them back into the city. And from above they poured arrows down on us like snow and slew about eighteen of your servants, and your servant Uriah was also killed among them.'"

And Joab's messenger came to Jerusalem before the king and told David the whole report of the battle. And David grew angry and was furious with Joab, and he said to the messenger all the words that he [Joab] had spoken beforehand [?]: "Why did you go so close to the wall of that city to fight, without caution? Did you not know that they would do you great harm from over the wall? Who killed Abimelech the son of Jerubbaal, son of Ner? Was it not one woman who threw a piece of millstone down from over the wall and killed him right there at Thebez? Now why did you go so near to the wall of that city?"

The messenger answered and said to David: "The fighting grew strong and fierce against us, for mighty men had come out from the city, and a strongly assembled band came out against us into the field. We turned them to flight and pressed them back to the gates of the city.
And the arrows from over the wall fell heavily on your servants, and about eighteen of the king's servants died, and your servant Uriah the Hittite was also killed with them in the same place."

David answered the messenger and said: "Say this to Joab: 'Do not let what has happened seem grievous in your eyes, for every battle goes sometimes one way and sometimes another. Now press the battle hard against that city and overthrow it!'"
When Uriah's wife heard that her husband Uriah had died in the battle, she lamented greatly and mourned for her husband.

When the days of mourning had passed, David sent for Bathsheba and brought her to his house, and she became his wife and bore him a son. And the thing that David had done before the Lord did not please the Lord.
And the Lord sent the prophet Nathan to David. And Nathan came to David and said: "I ask you to judge a case, so tell me: There were two men in one city; one was rich and the other poor.
The rich man had very many flocks and herds,

but the poor man had no flock, only one little lamb, which he had acquired and raised together with his children. It ate from his table and drank from his cup, and it rested in his bosom and on his breast. It was to him like his own daughter.

And it happened that a man came to the rich man as a guest. The rich man spared his own flocks and herds and would not take from them to prepare food for the traveler. Instead he took the poor man's lamb, slaughtered it, and prepared it for his guest."
When David heard this, he became very angry and said to Nathan: "As the Lord lives, the man who did such a thing deserves death.
And he shall repay the lamb fourfold, the man who did that deed and had no pity."
Nathan answered David and said: "You yourself are the one who did it! Now thus says the Lord God of Israel: 'I anointed you king over Israel and delivered you from the hands of Saul.

I gave you all the possessions of your lord and put his wives into your bosom, and I gave the whole house of Israel and Judah into your hands. And if that had seemed too little to you, I would have added still more for you!'

Now why have you despised and broken the command of your Lord, and done this evil deed before him? You killed Uriah the Hittite with the sword and took his wife as your wife, and him you killed with the sword of the sons of Ammon.
Now the sword shall not depart from your house for all time to come, because you despised me and took the wife of Uriah the Hittite as your wife.

Now thus says the Lord: Behold, I will raise up evil against you out of your own house. I will take your wives and give them before your eyes to another, and he will go in and lie with your wives openly before the sun.
You, who knows, perhaps thought that you did it [?] in secret; but I will do it openly before all the sons of Israel and before this sun.
David answered Nathan the prophet and said to him, "I have sinned before the Lord." Nathan answered David and said to him, "The Lord too has forgiven your sins, so that you shall not die!
But because you have greatly provoked the Lord your God to anger and have roused your enemies against you by this matter, now the child that is to be born of her shall surely die!"
And when Nathan had finished these words, he went away to his house. And the Lord struck with sickness the child that Uriah's wife had borne to David.
The child lay in distress. David prayed to God for the child and kept a fast. He had gone in and lay on the ground, clothed in sackcloth.
The elders of his people gathered to him and urged him to get up from the ground, but he would not get up, and he did not even sit down to eat bread with them at all.

And it happened that after the seventh day the child died. David's servants were afraid to tell him that the child had died. They said to one another, "While the child was still alive, we tried to raise him from the ground, and he would not listen to us or heed our voice. Now how can we dare to tell him of the child's death? Might he not do some harm to himself?"

When David saw that his servants were whispering something to one another, David understood that the child had died. And David said to his servants, "Has the child died?" They answered and said to him, "He has died!"

Then David rose from the ground. He washed and anointed himself, adorned himself, went into the temple of God and worshipped the Lord. Then he went into his house, sat down to eat bread, drank and rejoiced.

His servants said to him, "What is this thing that you have done? While the child was still sick, you fasted, kept vigil and wept; but when the child died, you rose up, refreshed yourself, made merry, ate and drank!"
David answered and said to them, "I have sinned [?]. While the child was still alive, I grieved and wept, thinking that perhaps the Lord would show mercy and the child would live.
Now that he has died, why should I grieve? Am I able to bring him back here? I am going to him, but he is not going to come back to me."
David called Bathsheba his wife and comforted her. He went in to her, and she conceived and bore a son, and he named him Solomon. And the Lord loved him.
He sent Nathan the prophet, and he named him Jedidiah, by the word of the Lord.
After this Joab fought against Rabbah of the sons of Ammon. He prevailed and captured their royal city.
And Joab sent messengers to David and said: "I have come; I have slain every fighting man of the city of Rabbah, and I have taken the quarter by the water!
Now gather the rest of your people and come to this city and take it, so that the capture is not called by my name but by yours."
He set out and came against the city of the people of Rabbah. He fought against it and took it.

And he himself took the crown from their king's head. Its weight was one talent of gold, with a precious carbuncle, and he set it on his own head. And he carried off a very great amount of plunder from the city.

And he brought the rest of the people out of the city. He sawed them with saws and killed them with [?] ("tabarak") and with iron [?] ("vazr"), and he brought them to Madibad, which is the place of the brick-makers. He did the same to every city of the sons of Ammon. And David returned with the people to Jerusalem.
And after all this it happened that Absalom, David's son, had a sister who was lovely and very beautiful, and her name was Tamar. And Amnon, David's son, fell in love with her.
And he was tormented because of her. He had collapsed and lay sick, distressed over Tamar his sister, and he could find no way to do anything to her.
And Amnon had a friend named Jonathan. He was the son of Shimeah, David's brother. Jonathan was a shrewd man.

He began to speak to Amnon and said: "Why are you like this? Why are you wasting away day after day, O son of the king, and you do not tell us?" Amnon answered him: "Tamar, the sister of my brother Absalom: I love her!"

And Jonathan said to him: "Lie down on your bed and pretend to be sick. And when your father comes to see you, ask him for her. Say to him: 'Send my sister Tamar, and let her attend me and feed me, and let her prepare the food in front of me, so that I may watch and eat from her.'"

And Amnon lay down on his bed and pretended to be sick. And when the king came in to see him, Amnon said to the king: "Command my sister Tamar to come in to me and prepare food for me, and I will eat from her hands!"
And King David quickly sent to Tamar's house and said to her: "Go to the house of your brother Amnon and prepare food for him!"

And Tamar went to the house of her brother Amnon, and he was lying stretched out on his bed. And Tamar took wheat flour and kneaded it with butter, and she took a board and made it into [?] ("lelango") in front of him.
And she put it on platters and held it out to him, but he did not want to eat. And Amnon said: "Send everyone out!" And when they had sent the men out,

then Amnon said to Tamar: "Bring that food into the bedchamber for me, and I will eat it there from your hands." And Tamar took the food she had made for her brother Amnon and brought it into the bedchamber.
And she held it out to him, and Amnon her brother seized her and tried to force her to lie with him.
His sister Tamar said to him: "Do not think this is right, my lord! Do not let this defilement happen, for such a thing has never been done in Israel. Do not commit this shameful, filthy deed!"

"For what place could there be that the shame of my disgrace would not reach? And you too would appear in Israel as one of the fools! So now, if you want anything, ask the king, my lord, for me, and know that he will not refuse you anything!"
But Amnon would not listen to her voice. He seized her, humbled her and defiled her.
Then Amnon hated her with a very great hatred, for that hatred was greater than his love for her had been. Amnon began to speak to her and said: "Get up and go away from here!"
"Do not do this, brother, for this last wickedness, driving me away from you today, is greater than the first thing you did to me!" But Amnon would not listen to her voice.
Then Amnon called his steward and said to him: "Send her away from me and shut the door in her face!"
Tamar was wearing a starred garment, for the daughters of the crowned ones wore such garments while they were virgins. Amnon's servants drove her out and shut the door behind her.
Tamar took ashes and put them on her head, and she tore the starred garment. She put her hands on her head and cried out with a great voice of lament, and she went along weeping.

Her brother Absalom met her and said to her: "What has happened? Why are you weeping? Has Amnon, my brother, done something to you against your will? Now be silent, for he is your brother, and do not take this matter to heart at all!" So Tamar lived like a widow, in grief, in the house of her brother Absalom.
When King David heard about all this, he was greatly grieved. But he did not want to trouble the spirit of his son Amnon, for he was his firstborn and he loved him very much.
From that time Absalom hated his brother Amnon because of his wicked deed, the defiling of his sister. Absalom did not speak a word to him at all, neither bad nor good.
After two years, Absalom held a sheep-shearing at Baal-hazor, which is near Gopher [Ephraim]. He invited all the king's sons.
Absalom came to the king and said to him: "Look, your servant is holding a sheep-shearing. Now let the king come to the house of his servant."
The king said to him: "Let it be, my son. We should not come and become a burden to you!" Absalom pressed him, but the king did not agree to go. Instead he blessed him and sent him away.
Then Absalom said: "Well then, send my brother Amnon with me!" The king said to him: "Why do you need him? Why should he go with you? [?] go about your business!"
Absalom pressed him, and he sent Amnon and all his sons with him. And Absalom held a great feast, like a royal banquet.

Absalom gave orders to his servants, saying: "Watch for when Amnon's heart grows merry with wine [?], and I say to you, 'Do it quickly.' Then strike him at once and kill him! Do not be afraid, for I am the one commanding you. Be strong and act like brave fighting men!"
Absalom's servants did to Amnon as their lord had commanded. Then all the king's sons got up, each mounted his mule, and they fled, each going his own way.
While they were still on the road, fleeing, a report reached the king. It said: "Absalom has killed all the king's sons, and not one of them has escaped."
David rose up quickly, tore his garments and sat on the ground. All his servants who stood around him tore their garments too.

Jonathan, the son of Shimeah, David's brother, began to speak and said: "Let my lord the king not think that all the king's sons have died. Only Amnon has been killed, for [?] had been laid up in Absalom's heart against Amnon from the day he violated his sister Tamar.
So now let the king not take it to heart that all your young men have perished. Only Amnon has been killed."

And Absalom fled. The watchman rose up as a lookout. When he lifted his eyes, he saw a great company coming along the road of Sorem, on the side of the mountain, on the descent. The watchman came in and told the king, saying: "I have seen a company coming down the road of Sorem, on the side of the mountain."
And Jonathan said to the king: "Behold, the king's sons are coming, just as your servant said, as I told you."

Just as he finished saying this, the king's sons arrived at once, crying aloud. They were lamenting and weeping, and they went in before the king. The king himself also wept, and he made all the people weep with a very great weeping.
Absalom fled from the presence of the king and went to Talmai, the son of Ammihud, king of Geshur, in the land of Chalmai. And the king mourned for his son all the days.
Absalom fled and went to Geshur, and he was there for about three years.
King David's heart ceased from going out against Absalom, for he had consoled himself over his son Amnon, who had died.
Joab, the son of Zeruiah, perceived that the king's heart had softened toward Absalom.

He sent to Tekoa and brought from there a wise woman. He said to her: "Make yourself a mourner and put on mourning clothes. Do not be cheerful, and do not anoint yourself with ointment. Instead, be like a woman who has mourned for a long time over someone who has died.
Then come before the king and speak according to these words." And Joab instructed her in the words that she was to speak with her mouth.
The woman of Tekoa came before the king. She fell on her face and bowed down to the ground, and she entreated him and said: "Save me, O king, save me!"
The king said to her: "What is it? What have you done?" The woman began to speak and said to him: "Truly I am a widow, for my husband has died.
Your handmaid was left with two sons. They fought each other in a field in the wilderness, and since there was no one to separate them, one brother struck his brother and killed him.

Now my whole clan has risen up together against me, and they say to me: 'Give us his brother, and we will kill him in return for killing his brother.' Now they intend to destroy him and quench the spark that is left, so that no memorial of my husband's inheritance would remain on the earth."
The king answered the woman and said to her: "Go to your house in peace, and I will give orders concerning you."
And the woman of Tekoa said to the king: "My lord king, let the sin be upon me and upon my father's house, and let the king and his throne be guiltless!"
The king answered and said: "Whoever spoke that word to you, bring him before me, and he will not touch you again."

The woman answered and said: "Remember, O king, the Lord your God, so that the kinsmen, the avengers of that blood, do not grow more and more numerous and destroy my son!" The king answered and said: "As my Lord lives, not one hair shall fall from your son's head!"
The woman of Tekoa answered and said: "Give leave for your maidservant to speak one word before the king, my lord!" And the king said: "Speak!"

The woman answered and said: "Why, then, has such a plan been devised against the people of the Lord? And this word has gone out from the king, to be confirmed by you, the king, that the one banished from you should not return?

For your son has died, and like water that is poured out on the ground and cannot be gathered up again, there is no longer any hope that his soul might return to him there. And now the king has resolved to keep the banished one away from himself.

And now, the reason I have come to speak this word to the king is that this people will see me, and they will say to your maidservant [?]: 'Let your maidservant speak before my lord the king, so that the king may do the word of his maidservant.'
So that the king may hear and deliver his maidservant from the hands of the men who seek to destroy me, all together, from the inheritance of the Lord.

And your maidservant said: 'Let the word of your lord the king be like an offering of sacrifices, for my lord the king is like an angel of the Lord in hearing good and evil!' And may the Lord your God be with you!"
The king answered the woman and said: "Do not hide from me a single thing I ask you!" And the woman said: "Let my lord the king speak!"

The king said to her: "Isn't Joab's word with you? Haven't you been put up to all the words you are saying?" The woman answered and said: "As your soul lives, my lord king, there is no turning to the right or to the left from all the words I am speaking, my lord king, for your servant Joab instructed me, and he put these words into my mouth to shape these words before you!
But you, my lord king, are yourself knowing and wise, like the knowledge of the angels of God, so as to know everything that is on the earth."
The king began to speak to Joab and said: "Look, I have granted you this request that you made to me. Go and bring back the young man Absalom!"

And Joab fell on his face to the ground, bowed down to him, and blessed the king. And Joab said: "Today your servant knows that I have found favor in your eyes, for the king has done what his servant asked."
And Joab got up, went to Geshur, and brought Absalom to Jerusalem.
And the king said: "Let him go and stay in his own house, and let him not see my face!" And he went back to his house and did not see the king's face.
And in all Israel there was no man as praised for his beauty as Absalom. From the sole of his foot to the top of his head there was no blemish in him at all.

And when he cut the hair of his head: from the beginning of the year until that time he would not cut his hair, because it grew heavy on him. When he cut the hair of his head, it weighed a hundred shekels by the royal weight.
And Absalom had three sons and one daughter. The daughter's name was Maacah, and she was very beautiful. Rehoboam, the son of Solomon, took her as his wife, and she bore Abijah.
And Absalom lived in Jerusalem for two whole years and did not see the king's face.
Absalom called Joab to him so that he could send him to the king, but Joab would not come to him. Then he sent a second time, and he still would not come to him.

Then Absalom said to his servants: "Look now, see: isn't Joab's plot near our estate? He has a [?] there sown with barley, [?ripe]. Go now, see to it, and burn it!" So Absalom's servants went and burned Joab's plot. And Joab's servants came with their garments torn and said to him: "Absalom's servants have burned the plot of our cultivated field."
And Joab got up at once, went to Absalom, and said to him: "Why have your servants burned the plot of my estate with fire?"

And Absalom said to Joab: "I sent to you once and said: 'Come to me, and I will send you to the king so that you can say to him: Why did I come from Geshur? I have come and I sit here. It would have been better for me to be there than to come and sit here without seeing the king's face. If there is any wickedness in me, put me to death!'"

And Joab went to the king and told him all these words. And the king ordered Absalom to be brought. He came in before the king and bowed down with his face to the ground. And the king called Absalom to him, embraced him, and kissed him on the face.
And after this Absalom began to acquire chariots and horses for himself, and fifty men to run before his chariots and horses.

And Absalom would rise early in the morning and come and stand by the road in front of the gates. Whenever a man had a case against his neighbour and was coming to the king for judgment, Absalom would call him over and ask him: "Where do you come from, and what city are you from?" And the man would tell him what lineage he was from: "Your servant is from the tribes of Israel."
Absalom would answer and say to him: "Look, your words are good and right, but there is no one before the king to hear what you would see fit to plead."
And then Absalom would say: "If only someone would appoint me ruler and judge over Israel [?]! Then every man who came to me for judgment, I would judge him with righteous judgment."
And whenever any man came near to bow down to him, he would put out his hand, draw him close, and kiss him on the face.
Absalom did this every day to every Israelite who came before the king for judgment. In this way Absalom won over the hearts of all the men of Israel.
And after the fourth year Absalom began to speak to the king and said to him: "Let me go and fulfil my vow, which I vowed to the Lord God in Hebron."
For your servant made a vow while I was living in Geshur of Syria, and I said: “If the Lord brings me back to Jerusalem, I will go and offer worship to the Lord in Hebron!”
The king said to him: “Go in life and in peace!” He got up and went to Hebron.
And Absalom sent messengers to all the tribes of Israel. He instructed them, saying: “When you hear the sound of the trumpet, all of you say together: ‘Absalom is king in Hebron!’”
And about two hundred chosen, notable men went with Absalom from Jerusalem. They went willingly and knew nothing of the plot, not a single word of it.

And Absalom sent and summoned Ahithophel the Gilonite, David's counselor, from his city [?] (“Metalad”). And while he stood and offered the sacrifices, the plot became firm and grew strong, and the people gathered to Absalom and grew in number.
And a messenger came to David and said to him: “The heart of every man of Israel is with Absalom.”

David spoke and said to his servants who were in Jerusalem: “Get up and let us flee from Absalom. Hurry and get out, for we will not escape him with our lives. Hurry and get away, or he may overtake us and destroy this city with the edge of his sword because of us.”
David's servants answered and said to him: “Here we are, O king! Whatever you wish, we will do.”
And the king himself went out on foot, with his whole household. And the king left ten women, his concubines, there to keep his house.
And the king went out on foot with all the people who were with him, and they came and stopped at a house some distance away.

And all his servants who were under his command gathered and went with him, and all the Cherethites and all the Pelethites gathered and arrived. They stopped under the olive tree toward the wilderness, and all the people were with him, and all the great men who were around him. And all the king's chosen warriors, about six hundred men who had come from Gath, passed on before the king.

The king spoke to Ittai the Gittite and said to him: “You are a foreigner and a stranger living among us. Why are you going into exile with us? Go back there and stay with the king, for you are a man who came to us for refuge as a stranger.

You only came to us for refuge yesterday and the day before. It is not right that today I should uproot you and take you with me, while I go wherever I may go. Go back there, and let your brothers go back with you, and may the Lord show you mercy and faithfulness.”
Ittai answered the king and said: “As the Lord lives, and as your soul lives, my lord the king, wherever my lord the king goes, whether to death or to life, there your servant will go too.”
The king answered Ittai the Gittite: “Come along and go with me!” And Ittai the Gittite got up and went on, together with all David's servants.

And King David, and all the people who were with him, and the whole land were blessing with a loud voice and weeping. All the people crossed over, and the king crossed the brook of Kidron, and all the people crossed over before him by the way of the olive tree, which is toward the wilderness.

And Zadok and all the Levites with him had taken up the ark of the covenant of God and were carrying it to Bethar. They set down the ark of the covenant of God until all the people leaving the city had finished coming out.

King David began to speak to Zadok and said to him: "Take the ark of the covenant of God back to the city, and let it stay in its own place. If I truly find favour before the Lord and he brings me back to his place, I will greatly see its beauty in my glory.
But if he says to me, 'You are not pleasing to me,' here I am! Let him do to me whatever seems pleasing to him."
The king said to Zadok the high priest: "See, take care, and go back to your city in peace. And here are Ahimaaz your son and Jonathan the son of Abiathar, your two sons with you.
And I, look, will stop and wait for you by the olive tree of the wilderness until word comes to me from you and tells me."
And Zadok and Abiathar took the ark of the covenant of the Lord back to Jerusalem and set it there.
And David went up the ascent of the olive tree, weeping, with his head covered. He went up barefoot, and all the people who were with him went with their heads bowed; they walked and wept.
And they came and told David, saying that Ahithophel too was a fellow conspirator and helper of Absalom. And David said: "May the Lord my God bring the counsel of Ahithophel to nothing."
And when David came to Ros[?] to worship the Lord, Hushai, his companion, was coming to meet David, with his garment torn and earth poured on his head.
David began to speak to him and said: "If you come with me, know that you will only be a burden to me there.

But if you go back to the city, say this to Absalom: 'Your brothers have gone away, and the king, your father. I wanted to come back to you. Now, O king, I am your servant; allow me, and I will live in your presence. Then I was your father's servant, and now let me be your servant.' And so you may somehow bring the counsel of Ahithophel to nothing.
And with you are Zadok and Abiathar the high priests. Whatever counsel you hear from the king, tell it to Zadok and Abiathar the priests.

And their two sons, Ahimaaz and Jonathan, are with them. Through them, let me know every word the king speaks. And say this to Absalom: 'Your brothers have gone away from us, and your father also has gone, but I left your father and came back, and now I am your servant.'"
And when Hushai, David's companion, entered the city of Jerusalem, Ahithophel too was with him.

And David had gone only a little way past Ros. And just then Ziba, the servant of Mephibosheth, was coming to meet him, and with him were two saddled pack animals[?], for on them lay two hundred loaves of bread, one [?] of raisins[?], two hundred fig cakes, and one [?] of wine.

The king answered and said: "What are these [?] (donkeys?) with their saddles?" Ziba said to him: "They are for the king's service. The bread, the fig cakes and the [?] are food for your servants, and the wine is for those worn out with thirst in the desert to drink."
The king said: "Where is your lord's son?" Ziba said to the king: "He is staying right there in Jerusalem. He said, 'Today or tomorrow the house of Israel will give me back my father's kingdom [?].'"
The king said to Ziba: "Behold, everything that belongs to Mephibosheth is yours." Ziba said: "I bow down to you, for I have found favor before you, my lord the king!"
King David came to Kora. A man from the kindred of Saul came out from there. His name was Shimei, son of Gera. He kept coming out, reviling and cursing.
He threw stones at David and at all his servants who were with him, while the whole band of fighting men walked on the king's right and left.
In his cursing Shimei said this: "Get out, get out, you man of blood, full of lawlessness!

Now, behold, the Lord God has brought back on you all the blood of the house of Saul, because you reigned in his place. The Lord has snatched away your kingdom and put it into the hands of your son Absalom. He has brought all your wickedness down on you, because you are a man of blood and lawless!"
Abishai, son of Zeruiah, began to speak to the king and said: "Who is this one contemptible dog who is insulting my lord the king? Just command me, and I will go and cut off his head."

The king answered and said: "What is there between me and you today, Abishai, son of Zeruiah? Do not stop him. Let him be. Let him revile me and curse me. Who knows? Perhaps the Lord has said to him, 'Rise up against David and revile him.' And who is there who could say to him, 'Why have you done this?'"

David began to speak to Joab, his commander, and to all the people, and said: "Behold, if even my own son, who came out of my belly, seeks my life, now this son of the Benjaminite has come and reproaches me. Let him be. He is cursing me. Who knows whether the Lord has spoken to me through him,
so that he may see this humiliation of mine and repay me with good in place of that curse?"
David and all the people went on along the road. Shimei went along the side of the mountain near them. He cursed, threw stones and flung dust.
The king and all the people who were with him came and arrived at the bank of the Jordan, weary and exhausted, and they rested there.
Absalom and all the people of Israel came and entered Jerusalem, and Ahithophel was with them.
When Hushai, David's friend, came to the city to Absalom, Hushai bowed down to him and said: "May King Absalom live forever!"
Absalom answered Hushai and said: "Is this the love between you and your friend? Why did you not follow your friend?"
Hushai answered and said to the king: "I have followed the one whom the Lord and all the people of Israel have chosen. I will be his, and I will remain with him!
Besides, whose servant am I? Should I not bow down to his son? As I served your father, so I will be before you."
Then Absalom began to speak to Ahithophel and said: "Take counsel and consider what we should do, so that we may be able to take possession of this land."

Ahithophel answered Absalom and said: "First, go in to your father's concubines, whom he left behind to keep his house. Then all Israel will see that you have shamed your father, so that your hands and the hands of the people who are with you may be strong."
So they set up a tent for Absalom on the roof, and he went in to all these concubines of his father openly, before all Israel.
The counsel Ahithophel gave in those earlier days was as if someone had asked God and God had confirmed it. That is how both David and Absalom regarded Ahithophel's counsels.
Ahithophel began to speak to Absalom and said: "Let me choose ten thousand men for myself and go down against David by night,
and I will fall upon them. I know that he is weary and his hands are slack. He will be frightened and all the people will flee, and I will overtake the king and kill him alone.
Then all the people will come back to you, as a bride comes back to her bridegroom. Pursue only him, and all the people will have peace."
This word seemed good to the king and to all the elders of Israel.
Absalom answered and said: "Call Hushai the Archite as well, and let us hear from him too what he will say."
So Hushai came in before King Absalom. Absalom told Hushai all of Ahithophel's words and said: "Now, should we follow this word of Ahithophel or not? What do you say?"
Hushai answered Absalom and said: "The counsel Ahithophel has given is not good."

Hushai went on speaking to the king and said: "You yourself know, O king, how brave your father is, and the people who are with him. They are brave men and warriors, bitter and enraged in heart like wild beasts in a fury out in the field. Your father is a brave and chosen man. He will not rest, and he will not let the people slip from his hands.

Even now he must be hidden and lying in ambush in some ravine or some other place. When you attack them, he will wake and rise up and cut down your people in a great slaughter. Then whoever hears of it will say: 'A great slaughter has taken place among the people who followed Absalom.'

Will anyone's heart then be brave in the fight, like a lion's? The heart of your people will be utterly broken and will completely give way, and all Israel will see that your father has prevailed over you.
But this is my counsel to you: when the whole house of Israel has gathered to you from Dan to Beersheba, when they are assembled like the sand of the sea in number, and you are in their midst,
then let us advance against them wherever we find them. There let us fall on them suddenly, as the morning dew settles on the face of the earth, and we will not leave even one man of them.

If he takes refuge in one of the cities, let them divide it among themselves by lot, surround it, take it and destroy that city completely, and drag [?] them into a ravine, so that they no longer find any other place to gather."

Absalom and all Israel answered and said: "This counsel of Hushai the Archite is better than the counsel of Ahithophel." For the Lord himself had ordained that the counsel of Ahithophel and the counsel of Absalom should be brought to nothing, so that the Lord might bring all that evil upon Absalom.
And Hushai began to speak to Zadok and Abiathar the priests, and said to them: "This is the counsel Ahithophel gave Absalom and all the elders of Israel, but this is the counsel I gave."
"Now act quickly: send and tell this to the king, so that he does not go toward the west [?] tonight through the wilderness, but so that they cross over the rivers and make camp there in safety."

Jonathan and Ahimaaz were waiting by the water of Rogel. A maidservant came and told them this, so that they could go and report the message to King David, because they could not openly enter the city and hear the message.

But one of the young men saw them, and went in and told all this to Absalom. So the two left very quickly and went into the house of a certain man in Beth-horon. That man had a pit in his courtyard, and the two of them went down into it.
And a woman took a cover and put it over the pit, spread a cloth over it, and was drying fig cakes on it.

At that very moment Absalom's servants arrived. They came in to the woman and said to her: "Where are Ahimaaz and Jonathan?" The woman said to them: "They came in quickly and went out again, and I do not know where they went!" They searched for them but did not find them, and went back to Jerusalem.

When the men had left, the two came up out of the pit and went and told all this to King David. They said to him: "Get up very quickly and cross these rivers, because this is the counsel Ahithophel is making against you!"
So David got up very quickly, together with the men who were with him, and they crossed the Jordan all through the night, so that their plan would not become known.

When Ahithophel saw that his counsel had come to nothing and had not been carried out, he quickly saddled his [?] (mount) and went home to his own city. He gave orders to his household, then went and strangled himself, and died. And they buried him in his father's house.
And David went on and reached his camp, and Absalom crossed the river Jordan, he himself and all Israel with him.

Absalom appointed Amasa commander over his people in place of Joab. Amasa was the son of Jether the Israelite, who had gone in to Abigail, the daughter of Jesse, the sister of Zeruiah (Georgian: Sharoel) and the sister of Joab's mother.
And Absalom came and made camp in the land of Gilead.

When David reached his camp, Shobi the son of Nahash came to him from Rabbah of the Ammonites, along with Machir the son of Ammiel, who was from Lo-debar, and Barzillai the Gileadite, who was from Rogelim.
They brought him ten beds, ten [?], ten cauldrons, [?], and ten earthenware vessels, as well as wheat and barley, flour, roasted grain, lentils, and [?].

They also brought honey and butter, sheep, and roasted calves, and presented all of it to David and his people to eat. For they said: "They are hungry and thirsty, exhausted and worn out in the wilderness."
At that time David [?] and reviewed his people, and set over them commanders, commanders of thousands and commanders of hundreds, and divided all the people into three companies.
